During a game, an adult in the bleachers slumps over and slides to the floor. They don't move when people call their name.
Make sure the scene is safe. Press Enter to place this card.
Tap their shoulders and shout "Are you okay?"; look for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds (gasping is not normal breathing). Press Enter to place this card.
Call 911 on speaker and send someone for the AED. Press Enter to place this card.
Push hard and fast in the center of the chest, 100 to 120 a minute. Press Enter to place this card.
When the AED arrives, turn it on and follow its voice prompts. Press Enter to place this card.
Keep going until help takes over or the person starts to move or breathe normally. Press Enter to place this card.
Wait a minute to see if they wake up before calling. Press Enter to place this card.
Stop every few compressions to check them. Press Enter to place this card.
Your friend suddenly grabs their throat. They can't talk, cough or breathe.
Ask "Are you choking? Can I help?". Press Enter to place this card.
Have someone call 911. Press Enter to place this card.
Give 5 back blows between the shoulder blades, then 5 abdominal thrusts just above the belly button. Press Enter to place this card.
Keep repeating until the object comes out or they can breathe, cough or talk. Press Enter to place this card.
If they stop responding, lower them to the ground and start CPR. Press Enter to place this card.
Give them water to wash it down. Press Enter to place this card.
Reach blindly into their mouth. Press Enter to place this card.
A classmate cut their forearm on a tool. It's bleeding a lot, and the teacher is across the room.
Put on gloves from the first aid kit. Press Enter to place this card.
Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or gauze. Press Enter to place this card.
Send someone to call 911 for heavy bleeding. Press Enter to place this card.
Keep the original pad in place. If blood soaks through, you can add one more pad on top and press harder. Press Enter to place this card.
Keep firm pressure until help takes over. Press Enter to place this card.
Lift the cloth every few seconds to check. Press Enter to place this card.
Take off the soaked cloth and start over. Press Enter to place this card.
A classmate grabs a hot pan handle. Their palm is red and a blister is starting.
Cool the burn under cool running water for at least 10 minutes. Press Enter to place this card.
Gently take off rings or anything tight near the burn. Press Enter to place this card.
Tell the teacher and school nurse about the burn. Press Enter to place this card.
Cover it loosely with a clean, dry, nonstick dressing. Press Enter to place this card.
Have a health care provider check the hand burn. Press Enter to place this card.
Put ice on it. Press Enter to place this card.
Pop the blister. Press Enter to place this card.
Hot August practice. A teammate is confused, stumbling, and their skin is very hot.
Notice the danger signs: confusion and very hot skin can mean heat stroke, an emergency. Press Enter to place this card.
Call 911 and tell the dispatcher about the heat stroke signs. Press Enter to place this card.
Move them to a cooler place, in the shade or inside. Press Enter to place this card.
Cool them fast in a cold-water tub up to the neck if available; otherwise use cold wet towels and ice packs. Press Enter to place this card.
Stay with them until help arrives. Press Enter to place this card.
Give them a drink while they're confused. Press Enter to place this card.
Let them rest alone in the locker room. Press Enter to place this card.
A student falls to the floor. Their body is stiff and jerking.
Stay calm and stay with them. Send someone for the nurse and call 911 if their seizure history is unknown. Press Enter to place this card.
Move hard or sharp things away. Press Enter to place this card.
Start timing the seizure. Press Enter to place this card.
Put something soft under their head and gently turn them onto one side. Press Enter to place this card.
Call 911 for a first seizure, injury, trouble breathing or waking, another seizure, or one lasting over 5 minutes. Press Enter to place this card.
Stay until they are fully awake, and talk to them calmly. Press Enter to place this card.
Hold them down. Press Enter to place this card.
Put something in their mouth. Press Enter to place this card.

Check, Call, Care. Check that the scene is safe, then check the person. Call 911 (or send someone) when it is serious. Care for the person until help takes over.

When to call 911. Someone isn't responding or isn't breathing normally, can't breathe, has heavy bleeding that won't stop, has signs of heat stroke, or you're not sure. For seizures, call for a first seizure or unknown history, injury, trouble breathing or waking, another seizure, or over 5 minutes. Also call for a seizure in water, during pregnancy, or with diabetes and loss of consciousness. Put the phone on speaker so your hands are free.

Hands-only CPR. For a teen or adult who suddenly collapses: call 911, then push hard and fast in the center of the chest, 100 to 120 a minute, at least 2 inches deep, letting the chest come all the way up. Don't stop until help takes over. For infants and young children, a class teaches CPR with breaths.

AEDs. An AED is a portable device that can check the heart's rhythm and give a shock if needed. Turn it on and follow its voice prompts; it won't shock someone who doesn't need it. Many schools and gyms have one: find yours.
Good to know. A class with a manikin teaches depth, hand position and how it feels. The American Heart Association and the American Red Cross offer them, and many schools teach hands-only CPR.
